sections.title: Role and Definition of EVM
sections.text: Error Vector Magnitude is the primary metric utilized in modern wireless communication systems to evaluate the quality of modulation [2] [1]. It is fundamentally defined as the Root Mean Square (RMS) amplitude of the error vector [2]. This metric allows for a quantitative assessment of how closely a transmitted signal matches its ideal form, serving as a standard benchmark for modulation performance [1].

sections.title: Signal Comparison Methodology
sections.text: The calculation of EVM relies on a direct comparison between two distinct signals: a reference signal and a test signal [1]. The test signal typically represents the actual output, which is generated by passing the reference signal through various functional blocks such as amplifiers, filters, mixers, or converters [1]. In some cases, the test signal may represent the output of a complete system, such as a transmitter [1]. This comparative approach isolates the distortions introduced by the hardware or system under test [1].

sections.title: Measurement Instrumentation and Processing
sections.text: Practical EVM measurements are commonly executed using specialized instruments like vector signal analyzers or real-time analyzers [3]. These devices capture a time-domain record of the signal and internally perform a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to facilitate the analysis [3]. A critical preprocessing step in this workflow involves down-converting the signals before the final EVM calculations are performed [3]. This ensures that the complex baseband values are correctly represented for accurate error vector determination [3].

sections.title: Normalization Across Modulation Types
sections.text: When applying a general equation for EVM across different modulation types such as BPSK, QPSK, or MQAM, it is essential to account for the inherent differences in signal amplitude levels [3]. Different modulation systems utilize distinct amplitude scales, which means that raw error values are not directly comparable without adjustment [3]. To ensure that EVM measurements are calculated and compared effectively across these varied systems, a normalization process is typically required [3]. This step standardizes the metric, allowing for a fair assessment of modulation quality regardless of the specific constellation size or type [3].

question: Does active learning work well when fine-tuning large language models?

sections.title: Sample Size Limitations
sections.text: A primary obstacle to applying active learning for fine-tuning large language models is the insufficient volume of data typically generated by these strategies. Most active learning methods produce datasets that are too small, often consisting of only hundreds of samples, to support the feasible fine-tuning of large deep language models [1]. This scarcity of training data exacerbates existing risks associated with fine-tuning, such as over-fitting, which is particularly pronounced when training sets are small [1]. Consequently, the limited data volume inherent in standard active learning loops poses a significant challenge to the effective adaptation of large-scale models.

sections.text: The quality of the selected data is critical, as common retrieval-based selection methods often fail to optimize diversity. Nearest neighbor retrieval approaches, for instance, tend to select redundant data points, which can limit the effectiveness of the selection process or even degrade model performance [2]. To address these issues, newer algorithms like SIFT have been introduced to reduce uncertainty regarding the model's response to specific prompts [2]. By focusing on uncertainty reduction rather than simple similarity, such methods aim to select more informative data points that better guide the fine-tuning process.

sections.text: Active learning and fine-tuning must also account for the risk of perpetuating or amplifying biases present in the source data. As a result, fine-tuned models may continue to perform poorly for under-represented groups if the data selection process does not explicitly address these disparities.

question: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) receivers can provide a reference clock signal known as Pulse-per-Second (PPS or 1-PPS). Is the PPS physically generated through a digitally-controlled oscillator (or line driver) whose offset is periodically re-initialized by the estimated clock bias (retrieved by means of PVT algorithms)?

sections.title: PPS Generation and Coherence
sections.text: Standard GNSS receivers deliver a time reference primarily through their Pulse-per-Second (1PPS) output [2]. This signal is not generated in isolation; rather, the 10 MHz frequency output from the GNSS system follows the 1PPS coherently [2]. Consequently, the time derivative of the 1PPS phase remains consistent with the output frequency [2]. While the specific phase relationship between the PPS and the 10 MHz signals may be unknown, this uncertainty is rendered irrelevant because the offset is strictly bounded within ±1 ns [2]. In specialized setups, such as those using a Quartzlock E80-GPS disciplined rubidium oscillator, the reference PPS is generated to ensure full synchronization between transmitting and receiving sides [1]. Similarly, on the receiving end, devices like the GNSS RTK Receiver GINTEC M1G2 generate the PPS signal [1].

sections.title: Offset Characteristics and Corrections
sections.text: The GPS 1PPS signal exhibits an offset from the true GPS second of up to 50 ns [5]. To mitigate this discrepancy, the receiver provides a periodic correction for this offset [5]. In high-precision applications, such as those utilizing a Spectracom 1200-233 multi-GNSS referenced rubidium oscillator, the system achieves a stability of 1 parts-per-trillion on the 10 MHz output and maintains an accuracy of ±25 ns when locked to the 1 PPS [4]. Furthermore, GNSS receivers record data that allows for the reconstruction of the phase error of the rubidium oscillator relative to GNSS time, thereby enabling further postcorrection of the frequency offset [3].

sections.title: Digital Control and FPGA Implementation
sections.text: FPGA-based autonomous GPS-disciplined oscillators have been proposed for use in wireless sensor network nodes [2]. In these systems, the 1PPS signal serves as the phase reference for a counter block, which in turn produces the sampling clock [2]. To maintain precision, a temperature sensor collects values from the oscillator on the board [2]. These temperature readings are utilized by an adaptive algorithm running on a Microblaze processor to compensate and adjust the control parameters for the 1PPS module [2]. This digital approach allows for the fine-tuning of the oscillator's behavior in response to environmental changes.

question: During pre-training, why is the transformer embedding layer initialized randomly, rather than with pre-trained embeddings from existing models?

sections.title: Absence of Explicit Rationale in Literature
sections.text: The specific question of why transformer embedding layers are initialized randomly during pre-training, rather than with pre-trained embeddings such as word2vec or GloVe, is identified as a mechanism and design-rationale inquiry. However, a comprehensive review of available findings indicates that no records directly address this specific preference for random initialization over pre-trained embeddings in the context of transformer pre-training. Searches for definitions and mechanisms related to embedding initialization yielded no relevant records, and external papers identified in the search did not provide a direct answer to the 'why' behind this design choice. Consequently, the provided claims do not contain a definitive statement explaining the theoretical or empirical superiority of random initialization for the initial pre-training phase.

sections.title: Distinction Between Pre-training and Continued Pre-training
sections.text: While the initial rationale for random initialization is not explicitly detailed, the DEPT paper provides insights into how models are handled during continued pre-training, which distinguishes between randomly initialized and pre-initialized models [1]. For models that are initialized randomly during this continued phase, the training process begins with a maximum learning rate and decays over a set number of steps [1]. This decay schedule is designed to allow for the rapid learning of the embedding matrix without necessitating another full training pass [1]. In contrast, when using models that are already pre-initialized, the learning rate starts at half of the maximum value because both the model weights and the embeddings are considered reasonably well-trained [1]. This suggests that the training dynamics and hyperparameter schedules differ significantly depending on whether the embeddings start from a random state or a pre-trained state.

snippets: When using pre-initialized models, we start from $\eta_{\mathrm{max}} / 2$ since both the model and embeddings are reasonably well-trained.

During continued pre-training, for models initialized randomly, we begin with $\eta_{\mathrm{max}}$ and decay over $N_{\mathrm{CT}}$ learning steps, allowing quick embedding matrix learning without requiring another full training pass, as is common in language rewiring (Artetxe et al., 2020).

sections.title: Pre-training as a Generalization of Word Embeddings
sections.text: The evolution of transformer models is linked to the success of earlier pre-trained word embeddings, which motivated the development of more generalized models capable of providing pre-trained weights across all layers of the network [3]. This historical context highlights a shift from static word embeddings to contextualized representations. In standard deep neural networks, a word embedding layer is typically included at the beginning of the architecture, a structure also observed in models like LSTMs and CNNs [2]. The transition to transformers involved integrating these embedding layers into a more complex architecture where the embeddings are learned jointly with the rest of the model during the pre-training process, rather than being fixed inputs from a separate pre-training stage.

sections.title: Contextual Representation and Task Mismatch
sections.text: The design of transformer pre-training, specifically through masked language modeling, forces the encoder to maintain a distributional contextual representation of every input token [5]. This is because the model does not know which words will be asked to be predicted or which have been replaced, ensuring that the embeddings capture rich contextual information [5]. However, this pre-training objective creates a mismatch with fine-tuning tasks, as the masking token used during pre-training does not appear during fine-tuning [5]. Additionally, the static nature of token embeddings in original BERT models has been identified as a drawback, contributing to issues with sentence embedding quality [4]. These factors suggest that the embedding layer must be highly adaptable and context-dependent, which may be better achieved through end-to-end learning from random initialization rather than relying on static pre-trained vectors that may not align with the specific contextual demands of the transformer architecture.

sections.title: Domain-Specific Initialization Practices
sections.text: In specific domains, it is common practice to initialize models from existing pre-trained models and then perform further pre-training to adapt them to new data [6]. Models such as BioBERT, ALeaseBERT, TOD-BERT, HateBERT, infoXLM, and XNLG are examples of this approach, where they are obtained by initializing from existing pre-trained models and then undergoing additional pre-training [6]. This practice is distinct from the initial pre-training of a general-purpose transformer, where the embedding layer is typically initialized randomly. The existence of these domain-specific models, which leverage pre-trained weights, further underscores that the choice of initialization strategy depends on the stage of training and the specific goals of the model, with random initialization being the standard for the foundational pre-training phase.
